worked_solution:
A differential equation of the form

$$
P(r,s)\,\text{d}r+Q(r,s)\,\text{d}s=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂s}=\frac{∂Q}{∂r}.
$$

For the equation $(1-s{e}^{rs})\,\text{d}r+(-r{e}^{rs}+4s)\,\text{d}s=0$, we have  

$$
P(r,s)=1-s{e}^{rs},\,Q(r,s)=-r{e}^{rs}+4s.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂s} & =\frac{∂}{∂s}(1-s{e}^{rs}) \\  & =-\,({e}^{rs}+rs{e}^{rs}),\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂r} & =\frac{∂}{∂r}(-r{e}^{rs}+4s) \\  & =-\,({e}^{rs}+rs{e}^{rs}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂s}=\frac{∂Q}{∂r},
$$

the exactness condition is satisfied. Therefore, the given differential equation $\text{is exact}.$
